question: Conservation of Energy
content: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only change form. In organizations, time, attention, and capital are finite resources; spending on one thing diverts from another.
description: A CEO diverts 30% of the engineering budget to a flashy rebranding campaign. Six months later, product quality drops and customer churn increases. The CEO is surprised. What principle explains this outcome?
options: The rebranding team was incompetent
Engineering should maintain quality despite the budget reduction
Rebranding diverted resources from product development
Marketing campaigns always damage product quality
answer: Rebranding diverted resources from product development
explanation: Organizational energy (budget, attention, talent) is finite. Every allocation is a trade-off. The CEO spent energy on rebranding, which necessarily meant less energy for engineering. There are no energetic free lunches — resources diverted from one area must be subtracted from another.

question: Entropy
content: The Second Law of Thermodynamics states that in any closed system, disorder (entropy) naturally increases over time. To reverse or slow entropy, you must inject external energy.
description: A codebase that was clean and well-organized at launch is now a tangled mess of technical debt two years later, even though the same team has been maintaining it. What natural force explains this degradation?
options: The developers became lazy over time and stopped maintaining standards
Poor management allowed corners to be cut
Entropy — systems naturally become more disordered without energy input
The codebase grew too large for any team to maintain
answer: Entropy — systems naturally become more disordered without energy input
explanation: Entropy is the natural tendency toward disorder. A clean codebase does not stay clean automatically. It requires continuous deliberate effort — refactoring, code reviews, documentation updates — just to maintain order. Without that energy injection, chaos is the default state.

question: Energy Trade-offs
content: Because organizational energy is conserved, every strategic decision involves an explicit trade-off. Choosing A means not choosing B, C, and D. Denying trade-offs does not eliminate them.
description: A startup tries to pursue enterprise sales, consumer product, and platform marketplace simultaneously with a team of 15 people. All three initiatives fail. What went wrong?
options: The market was not ready for any of the three product offerings
The team lacked the skills required for any of the three attempted initiatives
Energy spread across three vectors, none received critical mass
The startup should have hired more people before attempting multiple initiatives at once
answer: Energy spread across three vectors, none received critical mass
explanation: With finite energy, splitting it three ways means each initiative gets a fraction of what it needs. Conservation of energy means you cannot do three things well with the resources for one. Concentrate energy on fewer vectors to achieve critical mass.

question: Maintenance Energy
content: Entropy never stops. Every system — relationships, codebases, fitness, organizational culture — requires continuous energy just to maintain the current level of order, let alone improve.
description: A manager cuts the 'non-essential' training budget, team-building events, and one-on-one meetings to save costs. Six months later, team performance and morale have dropped. What went wrong?
options: The team was overspending on perks and needed to be cut back
Those were maintenance energy needed to counteract organizational entropy
Team morale is not affected by budget cuts if the work itself is meaningful
The manager should cut other departments instead of these activities
answer: Those were maintenance energy needed to counteract organizational entropy
explanation: Training, team building, and one-on-ones look discretionary, but they are the energy injections that keep organizational culture and skills from degrading. Without them, entropy takes over: skills stagnate, relationships fray, and chaos increases. Maintenance energy is mandatory, not optional.

question: Closed Systems
content: A closed system receives no external energy and will inevitably reach maximum entropy. In business, a team or company operating in isolation — without new ideas, talent, or competitive pressure — will inevitably decay.
description: A once-dominant company stops hiring external talent, stops attending industry conferences, and stops reading competitor research. After five years, its products are irrelevant. What thermodynamic principle explains this?
options: The company became arrogant and stopped listening to customers
Closed system, no energy input — entropy maximized into irrelevance
The industry changed too quickly for any company to keep up
The company's founders retired and lost interest in the business
answer: Closed system, no energy input — entropy maximized into irrelevance
explanation: A company that closes itself off from external energy (new talent, ideas, competitive pressure) becomes a closed thermodynamic system. Without external energy injections, entropy increases until the system becomes inert and irrelevant. Open systems survive; closed systems decay.

question: Zero-Sum Resource Allocation
content: Because energy is conserved, allocating resources to one area is a direct subtraction from all others. Leaders who deny this reality create invisible deficits in the areas they neglected to fund.
description: A product manager insists the team can 'do it all' — build new features, pay down technical debt, improve onboarding, and expand to mobile — without sacrificing anything. What is the flaw in this thinking?
options: The team should trust whatever the product manager says about feasibility
Hours spent on one activity are hours unavailable for another
Modern engineering teams are capable of unlimited parallel output
Technical debt should never be prioritized over new features
answer: Hours spent on one activity are hours unavailable for another
explanation: Engineering hours are finite conserved energy. Every sprint hour allocated to features is unavailable for debt, onboarding, or mobile. Denying trade-offs does not eliminate them — it just means the deficits accumulate invisibly until they become crises.

question: Local vs Global Energy
content: You can concentrate energy locally to create order in one area, but only at the expense of increasing disorder elsewhere. Optimization in one subsystem often creates entropy in another.
description: To meet a quarterly deadline, a team cuts all testing, documentation, and code reviews. They ship on time. Two months later, bugs and confusion slow the team to a crawl. What happened?
options: The team should have anticipated bugs and allocated time to fix them
Local energy on deadline created global entropy now requiring more energy
The deadline was unrealistic and should have been pushed back
Testing and documentation are unnecessary if the team is experienced
answer: Local energy on deadline created global entropy now requiring more energy
explanation: By concentrating all energy on the local goal (shipping on time), the team neglected the maintenance energy that keeps the broader system orderly. The resulting disorder (bugs, confusion) is entropy that must now be paid back — often with interest.

question: Thermodynamic Kindness
content: Relationships, like physical systems, require continuous energy input to maintain their current state. Neglecting them does not preserve the status quo — it triggers entropic decay.
description: A former colleague was once a close collaborator. After not speaking for two years, you reach out and find the relationship feels distant and awkward. You expected it to stay the same. What explains the change?
options: The colleague changed as a person during those two years
Relationships follow entropy — without regular energy, they deteriorate
The colleague was never a true friend if the relationship degraded that quickly
Two years is not enough time for a meaningful relationship to decay
answer: Relationships follow entropy — without regular energy, they deteriorate
explanation: Relationships are not static. They require ongoing energy — messages, calls, shared experiences — just to stay in place. Without that maintenance energy, entropy takes over and the connection decays. This is not a personal failing; it is a natural law of human systems.
